div1.head: Interview with Shirlee Thompson and Charles Thompson [July 2, 2002]

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: July 2nd, 2002. I'm interviewing Margaret Shirlee Cluff Thompson and Charles David Thompson, and the interview is taking place in our home. My name is Kenneth Charles Thompson, and I'm their son. Okay. First we'll start out with Shirlee.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay, Shirlee, what is your birthdate?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Where did you live during the war?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I was born and raised in Detroit, and I lived there until I went into the service.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: And okay, so were you employed?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, I had several different jobs. I was going to Wayne University at the time. After high school graduation I worked for Thompson Products one summer. We assembled parts for Jeep repairs which were sent overseas.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What year was that?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I don't know. '42 or '43.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I also -- another summer I worked at Sherwin-Williams Paint Company in the chemistry department, and I got that job because I had high school chemistry. I really didn't know very much about chemistry, but there was such a shortage of qualified men that were available that women were able to get all sorts of jobs that otherwise they would not have been able to get.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Why did you choose that activity?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: On those particular jobs?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: They were available, and they paid well.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What did you like or dislike about them?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, the chemistry, I finally had to quit there because the fumes from the paint products made me ill, and I didn't like that. Thompson Products was very interesting because one of -- my great aunt worked there, and actually she got the job for me, and they had lots of activities for the employees: Picnics and bowling leagues and whatever, so actually it was kind of fun.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Were you unionized?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: They were unionized. I didn't belong to the union because I was a temporary employee.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How did you feel about unions?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, at that time I was very pro union because my father had worked in factories, and before the union came in it was very sad that they were treated very poorly, and the unions did a lot for the factory workers, and it changed my mind over the years; however, at that time I was very pro union.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you develop friendships during your employment?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Yes, I did in the various places I worked. The chemistry company -- when I worked for the chemistry department I really didn't develop long friendships. I had friendships with the people I worked there with, but nothing that was lasting.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you have family or friends in the service or doing war work, did you?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Yes. Everybody was either in the service -- my cousins were in the service. I didn't have any brothers, and most of my relatives were working in a lot of plants.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: And these questions are for Charles. What war did you serve in, and what was your age?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: World war II, and my age was -- when I entered the service I was 19.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What branch of the service were you?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I was in the Army.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What was your rank?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: My rank for most of the war was PFC. I was a corporal.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Where did you serve?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I served overseas in Europe in Belgium.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Were you drafted, or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I was drafted.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: In Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Why did you -- you didn't pick the branch you were in at the time? Did you pick the branch you --

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, basically I did. Yeah. I was asked, and I said infantry because I was young and foolish.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you recall the first days of service?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I went to boot camp, which I guess almost everybody did.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What did it feel like?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: The first days were just long lines and getting inoculated and getting your uniforms.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. Well, that's kind of what this question is. Kind of tell me about your boot camp training experiences.

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, boot camp was fairly rigorous. They, you know, took you out to the firing squad or you know, for practice with live ammunition, and they trained us how to disassemble and assemble our rifles and maintain them properly and various other skills. We went on a lot of long hikes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you remember any of your instructors?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Not from boot camp, no.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: And how did you get through it?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I got through it okay. There was no particular problem.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. Let's get back to Shirlee here.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How did you feel about the war?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, this is really probably a terrible thing to say, but my relatives had talked about World War I, and it sounded so glamorous that the stories that they told, and I thought it would be pretty exciting. I was young and very foolish at the time, and that was -- that was how I felt that it was really something.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What were your family or friend's feelings?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Quite different. My aunts and uncles who had boys who were very apprehensive and very sad because all these young kids who were going into the service.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you live with your family?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: In what ways did the war change your activities or habits?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, for one thing the shortages of food changed things quite a bit because we weren't able to get chocolate, bananas, some of the things, candy bars, ice cream was reduced to sherbet things that kids -- teenagers are interested in seemed like to be very important also. At the time I should have been learning how to drive. I couldn't because gas was rationed, and my father wasn't about to waste his coupons just to teach me how to drive, so that -- these are some things that were important to kids.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What were some of the changes in your life after the war started, pretty much what you talked about?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. There really weren't any huge changes, just minor ones.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What responsibilities did you take on?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I don't know that I took on any responsibilities.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: You were in the service?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: But that was later.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What social activities were you involved in at work or after work with co-workers?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, when I was going to Wayne University, we were entertaining soldiers and servicemen who were stationed in and around Detroit, and they would come to the university, and we would dance with them and have dinner, that sort of thing, on the campus.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How did you entertain yourself outside of work?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Movies was the big thing then. We went to lots of movies.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Tell me about shortages, of rationing of food and gas.

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I've already mentioned that about the food and the gas. Also shoes were rationed too, and that was kind of interesting because there was a lot of black market things going on. One of my friends worked for a shoe company, and he got me coupons for shoes, so I was able to get extra shoes which I shouldn't have been doing, but I did. And one of my aunt's relatives was kind of big shot in a gas company, and he got her extra coupons for gas which this is going on all over. We were always hearing about people who were getting extra coupons that they shouldn't be getting.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you have a vegetable garden or other ways to get food?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Oh, yes. We had a huge vegetable garden. There was a field next to our house, and my father had the whole thing planted, and when I was working for Sherwin-Williams every morning I would go out and pick fresh tomatoes and fresh lettuce and make a lettuce and tomato sandwich for my lunch, and I remember that because I loved the lettuce tomato sandwiches, and my mother canned fruits and vegetables which we would then had in the winter time.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How did you cope with war time shortages?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Just the way you cope with any shortages. What we could get we got, and what we didn't we did without.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How about talking about recycling rubber grease or other commodities?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: The biggest recycling I know is they would have drives. We would put in -- metal seemed to be what they were mostly concerned about. We would put in old toasters or whatever we could find that we could part with around the house in the way of metal.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. You talked on this briefly. To what extent was there hoarding or black market activities in the area?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: There was a lot of black market activity going on, and there was hoarding too. We had a closet in our house, and my mother had stocked up on sugar and flour because she remembered what it was like to be without those things during World War I, and -- so we got whatever we could, and the thing is it was so strange the way they did the rationing because children were allowed the same -- coffee was rationed, and children were allowed the same amount of coffee and sugar and meat as adults no matter what your age was, so obviously we -- two children weren't drinking coffee, but they were able to use those coupons to get extra coffee and whatever so.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How did you feel about the war -- war news from news reels or radio?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Again, at first it didn't really mean too much to me, but then as people I knew were being wounded or killed, then it got to be very personal.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. Let's go back to Charles.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: After boot camp where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I was in the ASTP which was -- they selected certain people through tests and other means to go to college and take courses that they wanted for particular jobs and applications. So I went to -- I was, of course in -- I was in Gelonica (ph), Georgia and completed that course, and then they sent me up to the University of Pittsburgh, I think.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What kind of course was that in Georgia?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, basically I think they were leaning towards electrical engineering. And I took a course in Pittsburgh. I was sent back to the -- to an infantry unit which was then the 78th Division.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you remember arriving and what it was like?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well arriving where?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: After boot camp.

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Oh, well, yeah. I remember arriving at the college there. We had it pretty good compared to most of the draftees, and when I went back to the 78th Division that was pretty tough. They were getting ready to go overseas. They were training pretty rigorously.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Where was that at? Where was the 78th stationed at?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: You know, my memory is very spotty. I don't remember whether that was -- I think my boot camp was in Georgia, and I -- It was somewhere in the South. Yeah, I think it was in Georgia also.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What languages did you speak?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, I spoke a little French, but I was not chosen for that.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. What was your job assignment?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I was basically infantryman. I was assigned to the weapons platoon.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you see combat?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, the food behind the lines was pretty good, but the -- When you got to the front lines, basically you got K rations and some C rations. As most people will tell you those were not the best eats.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I guess we had enough. I was never bothered by a lack of supplies except that the food wasn't too good.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family, writing letters?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I wrote some letters. When I was behind the lines, while in England anyway, I called some of my relatives there. My brother was stationed in England at the time.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you recall any particular humorous or unusual events?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, I -- There's a story I would like to tell when we were -- I don't know. Maybe this comes later, you know, when I was freed from the prisoner of war camp.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Go ahead and tell that.

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, I should probably relate my --

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. We'll talk about that later. This is still -- We're still talking about the front lines now. Did you feel pressure or stress?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, when I saw people dying I certainly did.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Could you tell me about how a day at the front is spent?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, in my station you're doing what you're told to do, and when you're told to advance or dig or whatever you're told to do you do. And since I was mostly with the orders we were trying to set up the proper positions and make sure that we had ammunition, enough ammunition and so forth. And we were told where to -- where to fire and you know, when to fire and so forth. But actually we were kept moving pretty much at the time that I was in the front.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What did you think of your officers or fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I thought they were all doing a job that they had to do, and they were -- I liked most of them.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. Let's go back to Shirlee.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you worry that our side might not win?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: No. I knew we would.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you know anyone who was wounded or killed in the war?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Tell me about corresponding via letters or otherwise to families or friends in the service.

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Oh, I had a tremendous correspondence going on. I wrote to many of my classmates, to most of my relatives who were in. And we were usually using what they call V-mail which was one sheet of paper that you wrote on, and it folded up and made into an envelope, and that's basically how we corresponded.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What effect did the war have on your physical and mental health of you or others?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I believe for myself I don't know that it had any effect, made any difference. I know that mothers who had children in it certainly affected them emotionally.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you think that medical care changed because of the war?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I don't know. It probably did, but I really don't know.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What was your most memorable experience or most humorous experience?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: During the war?

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: No. Well, I don't know. I can't really -- I can't really think of anything. Probably my most memorable one was when my friend and I were vacationing in New York City, and we were going to visit her -- We were staying in New York City, and we were going to visit her uncle who lived in Netcong (ph), New Jersey, and when we got down to the train station, just as we were to get on the train the gate slammed, and we couldn't get onto that train, and we had to wait for the next one. And that proved to be very memorable because on the train that we got on I met a soldier who was on leave, and we talked, and he asked me if he could come over to New York and visit while we were still there, and he did. And one thing led to another, and we ended up getting married.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Let's go back to Charles.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Were there many casualties in your unit?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes, there were several casualties, and I would say that most of our company and perhaps more than our company were captured by the Germans. That started the Battle of the Bulge.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Tell me a couple of your most memorable emergents?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, you know, I remember that we were asked to take a town that -- and we spent a good part of the day advancing toward the town, and finally the Germans retreated out of the town, and we took it and started to dig some fox holes, and then we had a bunch of tank destroyers which were really sort of canons on tank treads with us, and they had moved up with us, and then the command came for them to go back, and we were told to go back also because we could see the Germans forming up to make a counter attack, and we knew that they liked to do it at night, and we had previously dug fox holes from a position in which we were in before we captured that town, and our own officers considered those to be a much better defensive position, and we were going to get on the tank destroyers to ride back to our previous positions, but the order came for us to stay in the town and defend it. And our officers decided that the lines we started to dig weren't defensible and drew us back into the town and put us in several buildings which we tried to defend. We put our machine guns out behind some stone walls, and -- but in the dark, you know, it -- there was a lot of fighting, and then finally some German panzers rolled up, and basically we didn't have anything but some bazookas, and when they finally rolled into town and pointed their canon at our house and asked for surrender, and our officer decided to surrender us, and that's how I became a POW.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: That was the next question: Were you a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Tell me about your experience in captivity and when fed?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, when we were captured we were ordered to walk back, and I don't know how long we -- I guess we walked a good part of the day and a half or so to a railroad station, and there we went through a interrogation by the Germans which was pretty standard, I guess. We basically answered name, rank and serial number, and they didn't really -- at least me, push us. I don't know what they did to the officers because they segregated them. And then we were put on freight cars and moved to a Camp Lukenwald which was South of Berlin. And the food there was pretty bad, but I think all of us lost quite a few pounds while we stayed there. It was mostly we got, I think a slice or two of their worst bread in the morning and then some turnip soup at night.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you -- Is there something you would like to add?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Go ahead.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did your family know you had been captured?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: They were originally informed I was MIA, missing in action. And then they were informed that I was a POW.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Just recently I got the POW metal, and of course, I got the combat infantry badge.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: I'd like to touch on something that your wife mentioned. When your men were on leave, that was before you left for England?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: That was afterwards?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Afterwards.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: All right. Let me go back to Shirlee.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Were you a veteran?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What war did you serve in?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: World War II.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What branch of the service were you in?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: WAVES.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What was your rank?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Hospital Apprentice First Class.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Where did you serve?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Bethesda, Maryland at the National Naval Medical Center.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Were you drafted, or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Detroit.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I thought it was the thing to do.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Why did you pick the branch you joined?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Because my father had been in the Navy in World War I.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you recall your first days of service?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What did it feel like?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: It was quite an adventure. I think the Navy was treated very well. We were -- We took the train from Detroit to New York City, and we were stationed at Hunter College. We lived in apartments, and the Navy food was very good. We had classes, marched from place to place, but it was really -- It was an adventure.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. And when you were at Hunter College what was your job assignment?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, after boot camp then I went to training at Bethesda Hospital Corps, and after I completed the training I was awarded the first class, and then I stayed there and was stationed at Bethesda. That was kind of interesting because my boyfriend's father was working in Washington, D.C., for the OSS, and we would like to joke that he courted me. Chuck was back in North Carolina at the time, and we had every -- every week we had one night off while we were at Bethesda, and the one night we got to see first rate movies. My future father-in-law would like to come up and see the movies because there was no waiting in line. We just got in to see the movies, and he liked to do that. Then on the alternate times we couldn't leave the hospital grounds, but -- Well, that was when we couldn't leave, and then on the alternate nights when we could leave he would come and take me into town to some place for dinner, so I saw him every week.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. Let's go back to Chuck here.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. I was in Asheville, North Carolina. That was where they sent me after my leave when I -- I think we're getting ahead of the story.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Let's tell the story you were going to tell about when you were a POW.

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yeah. When I was a POW I said we were originally sent to a very large prisoner of war camp. It was like Lukenwald, and from there a small group of us was sent through Berlin at night on a train to a small town north of Berlin, Rheinsberg where they had a small prisoner of war. I wouldn't hardly call it a camp. It was just an installation, and to get there and get some better food we had agreed to do some work so that most days we did get fed better, and we went into the town to do various jobs. Usually they select five or six men to go and do a particular job that they wanted done. Most of it was manual labor of some type or other. In fact, all of it was manual labor of some type or other, and that lasted for a couple of months -- several months until we started hearing cannon fire in the distance, and we heard through the grapevine that the Russians were advancing toward Berlin. The guards who were guarding us were -- I'd say German men who were in their 60s and 70s, and they one night when we got -- when we woke up the next morning there were no guards, and we could hear the canon fire more distinctly. It was definitely not too far away, and one of our commanders said that he had heard that the Americans were just on the other side of the -- I think it was the Oder River, and that we were about 30 or 40 miles from there. So all of us took off walking, and I don't know how it happened, but when we were walking we found some Russian soldiers, and basically some of our people spoke Polish, and they communicated with them. One of them was a Serb also, enough to let them know who we were, and they were at that time just weren't too interested in us it seemed like. But we got to another -- we got to a town where -- that the Russians had captured, and apparently they had told the civilians there to bring all their bicycles to the center square of the town which the German civilians had done, and there must have been, you know, 50 or 60 bicycles piled up there in the middle of town, and we realized that we -- if we could get bicycles we'd have a much better chance of making it where we wanted to go. By this time, I don't really remember how, but we split into two or three groups, and the group I was with had people who could converse a little bit with the Russians, and they spoke to the Russian who was guarding the bicycles, and asked him if we could just take a couple of them or a few of them to get toward the Oder, and a guard shook his head, "No, no," he couldn't do that. But then he went and turned his back to us, so we took that as a sign, and we grabbed some bicycles and pedaled off as fast as we could go, and a couple hours later we made the Oder River where we saw there was a rubber raft down in a thing with some GIs -- down in the river with some GIs in it. And we motioned to them, and they came over, and we told them who we were and what we were. And they said they were going to go back and tell their officers, and some other boats were sent across, and we were ferried across the river, and that was from there we were sent to camps that took ex-POWs and people who were getting ready to be sent back to the States, and we were -- Actually I guess I went back to England first, and then I went back to the States, and they gave us two- or three-month leave, and it was during that leave part of the time I took some courses at Princeton University.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: It was during that leave when you met your wife?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: And so you were still in the service at that time after the war?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes. I was on leave.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: When --

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: And then from the leave I went -- I was sent back to Asheville, North Carolina which is where I was discharged.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What -- What year was it when you were discharged?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: It was '45.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: About how long after you left England were you discharged? I mean how long were you in the service after you got back?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I was on leave for several months, and then I think I was in Asheville for about three weeks or a month before I got discharged and I was completed.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: END OF SIDE ONE, BEGIN SIDE TWO.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: It was paid by the GI Bill?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did you make any close friends while you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I made one or two, but they weren't maintained.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: And did you join any veteran's organizations?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I joined the VFW directly after the war, but I didn't maintain that membership either.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. Let's go back to Shirlee.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Where were you on VE Day?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I was working at the Detroit News.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What did you do after the war?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, after the war I went back to college and was able to transfer to the University of Wisconsin. Incidentally I got married then went to the University of Wisconsin to finish up, and I got my bachelors degree from the School of Journalism there, and this was financed by the GI Bill.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: How would you describe the way the war changed your life or those of others?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I think for one thing my life and others too used to be that people kind of stayed where they were born. They more or less grew up there and stayed in the same area, but it seems after the war people scattered all over the country rather, and the nuclear family just kind of dissolved.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Is anything else I should ask?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Is there anything else you would like to add to the subject?

sp.speaker: Shirlee Thompson
sp.p: Well, I was a senior in high school when we were attacked by Japan. Many of my classmates went into the service after graduation. Some never returned. Because there were so many job vacancies it was easy for women to get employment. During school vacations I had various opportunities which I mentioned before working in the chemistry department of the paint company, and the only qualifications I had was high school chemistry, and I worked at Thompson Products, and I got that job through a relative, and that was a very boring job, but there was lots of activities that the company -- They did lots of things for the employees to keep the employees happy and I guess to keep them there because there were so many jobs available at that time that people just moved around. Then I worked part time for the Detroit News while attending Wayne University, and working there during war time was very interesting. Getting -- That was before television was at all in any of the homes, and so it was very exciting to get out extras. And all the things that you see in old movies going on in the newspaper offices really did happen at that time. I guess that probably is about it.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Okay. We'll go back to Charles.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: What did you do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, after I got my degree at the University of Wisconsin, and both of us got our degrees, my wife and I, then I was offered a job as a teaching assistant at Stanford University, and we came out to California, and then I got a job with United Airlines because things weren't working out too well, and we needed some more income, and then I got a job, but I don't think this is all related to the war.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Well, what did you do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: I was an accountant and auditor.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or the military in general?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Yes, it did; but basically I was happy that the war was over and that I got through it without any big injuries. And I was not interested in the military as a career.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Do you attend reunions?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Did the service affect your life?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: Well, it certainly did, the war, the World War affected my life, and the GI Bill affected my life. But, you know, I would say that's true of 95 percent of the people my age.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Is there anything that you would like to add that was not covered in this interview?

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: No. I think I've covered everything.

sp.speaker: Kenneth Thompson
sp.p: Well, future generations want to thank both of you very much for participating in this.

sp.speaker: Charles Thompson
sp.p: This is Charles Thompson. I would like to make one correction. The river where we met the Americans was the Elba and not the Oder, and I wanted to for anybody who was interested. Thank you.
